news.title: Anthropic的IPO：如何为AI未来定价？
news.snippet: Anthropic联合创始人兼CEO Dario Amodei透露公司计划IPO，引发投资者对其AI技术前景与估值的热议。
news.raw_snippet:
Co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei says Anthropic is going public because it needs more funding in its drive to develop cutting-edge AI — FABRICE COFFRINI / AFP

Speculation over Anthropic's stock market valuation has highlighted one of the riskiest bets in finance: trying to put a price on the future of artificial intelligence.

A few days before its initial public offering, the maker of the AI agent Claude said it was aiming for a market capitalization of up to $1.4 trillion. [...] A company's valuation is its share price multiplied by the number of shares outstanding. A company going public wants that price as high as possible, since it determines how much money it raises.

But it also has to leave enough room to attract buyers, since weak demand would drag down the stock.

Investors, for their part, want to be sure they can later sell their stakes at a profit -- and are hoping for a "pop," or sharp rise in the share price, on the first day of trading. [...] Speaking Friday with JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon, Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei cited a company motto when discussing the IPO: "underpromise and overdeliver."

He also said the company was going public mainly because it needs funding. Anthropic is set to raise a total of $90 billion through the offering, money it plans to use to develop cutting-edge AI.

news.raw_snippet:
# Should we give Anthropic 1.4 trillion US dollars?

The artificial intelligence industry is ushering in a landmark moment.

In November 2026, Anthropic, which was founded just over five years ago, launched its initial public offering (IPO), attempting to enter the capital market with a valuation of over US$1 trillion. [...] According to the information provided in the prospectus, the total basic circulating share capital of Anthropic after the completion of the IPO is approximately 130.7 billion shares. Based on the offering price range of US$70 to US$78, the corresponding base market value is approximately US$9.16 trillion to US$10.2 trillion. If approximately 49.2 billion potential shares such as employee stock options are included, the corresponding fully diluted valuation is approximately US$12.6 trillion to [...] However, Anthropic's listing not only represents the capital market's recognition of the prospects of artificial intelligence, but also means that a problem that has long been covered up by technological breakthroughs and financing booms must finally undergo public scrutiny: Artificial intelligence has created huge market demand, but can it really generate profits that match its valuation?

news.title: Anthropic IPO与Nvidia财报：一页速览本周AI要闻
news.snippet: Anthropic拟发行8.25亿美元A类普通股，Nvidia财报紧随其后，共同成为本周AI市场关注焦点。
news.raw_snippet:
Anthropic said it will offer $825M in Class A common stock in its upcoming IPO at a price range of $70 to $78 per share, valuing the company at about $1.3T to $1.4T.

It is targeting a retail allocation of about 20%, according to an updated filing, bridging this innovative artificial intelligence lab closer to the public. Typically, retail investors receive 5% to 10% of shares in a major U.S. IPO, so 20% is well above the norm, reflecting the listing’s status as a highly anticipated debut. [...] Once U.S. markets close on Wednesday, Anthropic and its lead underwriters plan to set the final IPO price. Over the past week, they have gathered institutional orders through a process called book building to establish a price reflecting real demand.

This pricing strategy has already undergone iteration; a draft filing initially suggested raising the valuation to $69.3B before being updated, reflecting the dynamic environment surrounding AI market valuations. [...] Demand continues to point upward, with sources indicating that orders are roughly six times oversubscribed. Some analysts suggest the initial target range was intentionally conservative.

Jeff Zell, senior research analyst at IPO Boutique, noted that pricing the valuation nearly 20% below initial market expectations gives investors space to bid up the shares naturally.

news.title: 人工智能：原创优势 | 德勤全球
news.snippet: 德勤指出，在APEC商业环境中AI虽已普及，但原创能力与差异化仍是企业构建持久竞争优势的关键。
news.raw_snippet:
Across APEC’s business landscape, with AI abundant but originality scarce, the organizations pulling ahead are redesigning the work, building on what only their people can do, and learning faster than their peers. Leading this change is the CEO’s job.

APEC economies and India

Artificial intelligence (AI) is profoundly reshaping the way work gets done across the APEC economies and India. [...] The organizations expected to pull ahead use AI not just to improve efficiency, but to redesign how their business creates value.

The human premium is rising.

As AI takes on more execution, advantage increasingly depends on how human judgement, creativity and insight is amplified by AI.

Original advantage compounds through deliberate learning.

Sustainable AI advantage comes from learning faster than competitors and turning every lesson into advantage that nobody can copy.

The CEO’s work [...] The CEO’s work

AI isn’t just a tech challenge. It’s about rethinking the business and its possible futures, defining what AI is for your organisation. The result is a company’s intelligence signature, and shaping it is the CEO’s work.

Simply having AI is no longer an advantage. It's the floor everyone stands on.

Robert Hillard, CEO, Deloitte Asia Pacific

news.title: 在Terry商学院，AI以人为本
news.snippet: Terry商学院强调，尽管AI工具日益强大，但人的创造力、判断力与伦理意识仍是商业教育与技术应用的核心。
news.raw_snippet:
Still, as impressive as those tools have become, it’s important for users — faculty and students alike — to be mindful of their limitations, says Schecter.

“There’s an analogy I use, which is to treat (AI) like an extremely competent intern,” he says. “You just hired this person, but they have no idea how to do the job yet. You tell them ‘I want this done,’ but if you don’t tell them how to do it, they’re gonna guess, and they might make a mess of things.”

### The Plan [...] In 1994, at the dawn of the internet age, Steve Jobs sat down with journalist Jeff Goodell for a Rolling Stone interview. The question was posed: do you have faith in technology?

“Technology is nothing,” the Apple co-founder mused. “What’s important is that you have a faith in people — that they’re basically good and smart, and if you give them tools, they’ll do wonderful things with them.” [...] Three decades after Jobs issued his rosy proclamation, the rapid rise of artificial intelligence is putting it to the test.

How does it feel?

“In my opinion, there’s a difference between the AI companies’ goals and what’s possible with the tool itself,” says Aaron Schecter, associate professor of management information systems and director of Terry’s undergraduate AI certificate program.

“People can do amazing things (with AI). But the problem is this thing’s coming on really fast.”
